summary: Coast Guard concrete tower of 1943 on the Avery Point campus in Groton: lit 1944, dark 1967, restored and relit by a society in 2006.

access.note: Grounds open on the University of Connecticut's Avery Point campus, with a memorial walkway open to the public. The tower is closed and its interior is not open to the public.

facts.agency: University of Connecticut (owner); Avery Point Lighthouse Society, a chapter of the American Lighthouse Foundation (operator)

events.note: State of Connecticut conveyed the Plant estate land to the federal government (deed dated 12 March 1942) for the Coast Guard training center
Octagonal concrete-block tower built 1943 from 1942 plans by Alfred Hopkins and Associates
Light established by Notice to Mariners of 3 May 1944; LighthouseFriends and the society give activation as 2 May 1944
Changed from fixed white (eight 200-watt bulbs) to flashing green at 200 candlepower
Light extinguished 25 June 1967 when the Coast Guard training programs relocated
Lighting apparatus removed from the lantern after discontinuance
Land returned to the State of Connecticut at no cost (LighthouseFriends; the nomination links the return to 1967)
Tower judged unsafe by the late 1990s; concrete blocks crumbling
Avery Point Lighthouse Society formed in February 2000 to restore and relight the tower
Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, 23 August 2002
Replica wooden lantern lowered into place 30 September 2005; balusters cleaned and reset
Relit as a private aid to navigation with a solar LED optic, 15 October 2006 ceremony (the society's page gives 24 September 2005)

corrections.why: The light was discontinued in 1967 and relit as a private aid to navigation in 2006 (LighthouseFriends; American Lighthouse Foundation; society page). The Coast Guard's list is not in the sources read.

The tower is owned by the University of Connecticut, a state university (nomination; LighthouseFriends). The Avery Point Lighthouse Society is the operator, a nonprofit chapter of the American Lighthouse Foundation.
The nomination gives the tower as 26 ft and the overall height including slab as 41 ft (about 12.5 m). The record's 16.8 m matches the 55-ft plane of the light, not the structure.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination links the return of the land to the Coast Guard's 1967 relocation; LighthouseFriends gives 1969. The story reports both.
The Notice to Mariners of 3 May 1944 announced the light; the society and LighthouseFriends give activation as 2 May 1944. The story gives the month and year, which all sources agree on.

The society's page dates the relighting to 24 September 2005; the American Lighthouse Foundation and LighthouseFriends date the relighting ceremony and private aid to 15 October 2006. The story gives 2006 as the relighting ceremony.
The NRHP listing record gives 23 August 2002; the American Lighthouse Foundation page says 2022 and is wrong.
LighthouseFriends attributes the delay to fears of an enemy sea invasion; the nomination gives no reason. The story gives LighthouseFriends' reason as its claim.

A popular account, repeated by the society, says the light was built as a memorial to lighthouses and keepers. The nomination shows that it rests on a 1955 misreading of the deed; the story follows the nomination.
The nomination says the original 100-candlepower light was visible up to seven miles; the record gives a 3.5 nautical-mile range for the current optic. Not reconciled here.

notes_for_editor: Thin on people and wrecks. No keeper, storm, wreck or rescue record was found for the light in the sources read; the chapters on keepers and storms are omitted. The USLHS place record lists the light as a minor aid to navigation with no people. Its coordinates (68 deg 12.28 N, 69 deg 3.35 W) are wrong (they fall in Maine); the record's own coordinates (41.315, -72.064) match LighthouseFriends, ARLHS and the nomination, so they were kept. The USLHS record also says 'Open to Public: No', which conflicts with the open grounds. The Coast Guard Historian's page for the light could not be read (live site blocked; archived copies not readable with the cache). The Groton Station News (1943) is cited only as the nomination quotes it; it was not read directly. A Chronicling America search for 1943-44 found nothing relevant. Not used: the Wikipedia article, which is lead-only; it gives an operator and a 1997 hazard finding that the story does not rely on. The current light's characteristic (Fl G 4s) is the society's and the foundation's description; no Coast Guard list entry was read. Verification pass 2026-10-22: the nomination's full text was searched for any reason given for the 1944 activation delay; none appears (no 'delay', 'enemy', 'invasion' or 'activated' in the text). The story takes the Groton Station News phrase ('a touch of Williamsburg') from the nomination's footnote 3 and does not claim to have read the paper. The USLHS place record's People link was not readable in the cache, so the story makes no claim about keepers from it; LighthouseFriends' 'never had a resident keeper' is the only keeper source. The society's history page gives $250,000 raised in an older appeal; the story uses the six-year, $500,000 restoration figure from LighthouseFriends and the American Lighthouse Foundation.
